claim: Cryogenic electron microscopy has become an essential tool for structure determination of biological macromolecules.
source: Cryogenic electron microscopy has become an essential tool for structure determination of biological macromolecules.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific consensus in the field of structural biology.

claim: The difficulty to reliably prepare samples with uniform ice thickness represents a barrier for routine high-resolution imaging.
source: In practice, the difficulty to reliably prepare samples with uniform ice thickness still represents a barrier for routine high-resolution imaging and limits the current throughput of the technique.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations throughout the manuscript discussing sample preparation challenges.

claim: A nanofluidic sample support with well-defined geometry can be used to prepare cryo-EM specimens with reproducible ice thickness from picoliter sample volumes.
source: We show that a nanofluidic sample support with well-defined geometry can be used to prepare cryo-EM specimens with reproducible ice thickness from picoliter sample volumes.
evidence: This is the primary experimental finding of the manuscript, supported by data presented in figures showing ice thickness measurements and sample preparation.

claim: The sample solution is contained in electron-transparent nanochannels that provide uniform thickness gradients without further optimisation.
source: The sample solution is contained in electron-transparent nanochannels that provide uniform thickness gradients without further optimisation and eliminate the potentially destructive air-water interface.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing thickness measurements and imaging results from the nanochannels.

claim: The closed channel architecture eliminates the potentially destructive air-water interface.
source: The sample solution is contained in electron-transparent nanochannels that provide uniform thickness gradients without further optimisation and eliminate the potentially destructive air-water interface.
evidence: This is a design feature of the device, supported by the description of the closed architecture and discussion of air-water interface effects.

claim: High-resolution structure determination is possible with three standard protein specimens using the nanofluidic chips.
source: We demonstrate the possibility to perform high-resolution structure determination with three standard protein specimens.
evidence: Demonstrated by the experimental results showing 3D reconstructions of apoferritin, T20S proteasome, and TMV at resolutions suitable for structural interpretation.

claim: A reproducibly thin and consistently uniform ice layer can often not be achieved with standard blotting methods.
source: A recognised shortcoming of this method is that a reproducibly thin and consistently uniform ice layer can often not be achieved (Carragher et al., 2019; Armstrong et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature discussing challenges in cryo-EM sample preparation.

claim: Time-consuming parameter optimisation is frequently required to find conditions suitable for high-resolution imaging in standard cryo-EM sample preparation.
source: Frequently, time-consuming parameter optimisation is required to find conditions suitable for high-resolution imaging, and these conditions are typically different for each sample.
evidence: This is a well-known challenge in the field, stated as established knowledge.

claim: Preferential orientation of particles is a problem encountered in cryo-EM sample preparation.
source: Even if such conditions are found, additional problems encountered in practice include preferential orientation of particles (Tan et al., 2017; Noble et al., 2018), preferential interaction of particles with the support film (Meyerson et al., 2014) and partial denaturation of particles due to exposure to the large air-water interface (Donaldson et al., 1980; Glaeser and Han, 2017; Glaeser, 2018; Noble et al., 2018; D'Imprima et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to literature documenting these issues.

claim: Partial denaturation of particles can occur due to exposure to the air-water interface.
source: Even if such conditions are found, additional problems encountered in practice include preferential orientation of particles (Tan et al., 2017; Noble et al., 2018), preferential interaction of particles with the support film (Meyerson et al., 2014) and partial denaturation of particles due to exposure to the large air-water interface (Donaldson et al., 1980; Glaeser and Han, 2017; Glaeser, 2018; Noble et al., 2018; D'Imprima et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to literature on air-water interface effects.

claim: The cryoChip consists of a 2 × 2 mm silicon base with 100 µm thickness.
source: The core design of this device, which we refer to as cryoChip, consists of a 2 × 2 mm silicon base with 100 µm thickness (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is a direct description of the device design, supported by Figure 1a showing the device schematic.

claim: A hollow microcantilever extends over the side of the chip base for sample application via capillary action.
source: A hollow microcantilever extends over the side of the chip base for sample application via capillary action.
evidence: This is a description of the device design feature, supported by figures and experimental demonstration of filling.

claim: The observation windows in the cryoChip are 6 × 4 µm in size.
source: Transversal silicon oxide layers provide mechanical stability and generate a regular grid of observation windows that are 6 × 4 µm in size (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is a specification of the device design, supported by Figure 1b showing the observation membrane.

claim: Sample thickness in cryoChips is controlled by the geometry of electron-transparent nanochannels.
source: Instead of wicking a suspended droplet to a liquid film thin enough for transmission imaging, sample thickness in cryoChips is controlled by the geometry of electron-transparent nanochannels itself.
evidence: This is a key design principle of the device, supported by experimental measurements of ice thickness.

claim: The closed channel architecture avoids the air-water interface, which is replaced by a solid-liquid interface between the SiNx membrane and the sample solution.
source: The closed channel architecture avoids the air-water interface, which is replaced by a solid-liquid interface between the SiNx membrane and the sample solution.
evidence: This is a description of the device design and its functional consequence.

claim: CryoChips are fully compatible with the most frequently used cryo-EM sample carrier cartridges with minimal adaptions.
source: With minimal adaptions, cryoChips are fully compatible with the most frequently used cryo-EM sample carrier cartridges (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2 showing mounting in different cartridge types.

claim: The average thickness of the silicon nitride layer is 9.5 ± 0.2 nm.
source: Using ellipsometry we measured a film thickness of 9.5 ± 0.2 nm for the final SiNx layer (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is a direct measurement result from ellipsometry, shown in Figure 1d.

claim: The combined water-equivalent thickness of the two SiNx membranes forming the nanochannel is 39 nm.
source: From the zero-loss log ratio of a SiNx area adjacent to the nanochannel (0.89) and the geometric film thickness determined by ellipsometry (19 nm, corresponding to the combined thickness of top and bottom membrane), we calculated the mean free path for inelastic scattering (IMFP) at 300 keV in SiNx as 163 nm, from which we estimate a combined water-equivalent thickness of 39 nm for the two SiNx membranes forming the nanochannel assuming an IMFP of 320 nm for vitreous ice (Yesibolati et al., 2020).
evidence: This is calculated from experimental measurements using zero-loss imaging and ellipsometry.

claim: The nanochannels display a concave profile in cross-section with a maximum thickness of ~100 nm at the channel wall and 0 nm at the channel center.
source: The channels display a concave profile in cross-section, leading to a gradient with a maximum thickness of ~100 nm at the channel wall and 0 nm at the channel center.
evidence: This is determined from ice thickness mapping using zero-loss imaging and tomography.

claim: The width of the nanochannels can range from 650 nm to 1000 nm between different chips.
source: The width of the nanochannels is consistent across individual chips, but can range from 650 nm to 1000 nm between different chips which we attribute to process variability and/or the chip position on the wafer during fabrication (Figure 1f).
evidence: This is measured from multiple chips and shown in Figure 1f.

claim: The total filling volume of the cryoChip is estimated to be ~4 pL.
source: From the geometry of the overall channel design, we estimate the total filling volume to be ~4 pL (see Materials and methods), which is about six orders of magnitude less compared to typical sample volumes of conventional blotting-based methods.
evidence: This is calculated from the geometric dimensions of the channels described in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The filling volume of cryoChips is about six orders of magnitude less compared to typical sample volumes of conventional blotting-based methods.
source: From the geometry of the overall channel design, we estimate the total filling volume to be ~4 pL (see Materials and methods), which is about six orders of magnitude less compared to typical sample volumes of conventional blotting-based methods.
evidence: This is a comparison based on the calculated filling volume and known volumes for conventional methods.

claim: The movement of the liquid front during filling is proportional to the square root of time, in accordance with Washburn kinetics.
source: We observed the movement of the liquid front to be proportional to the square root of time, which is in accordance with classical Washburn kinetics for capillary flow (Washburn, 1921).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental measurements of filling kinetics shown in Figure 2d, and supported by citation to Washburn's work.

claim: Complete filling of the entry channel proceeds at an average of ~1 mm/s.
source: Filling is rapid and complete filling of the entry channel proceeds at an average of ~1 mm/s (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is measured from kymographs of the filling process shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The entire filling process can be executed in a lab environment without humidity control.
source: The entire filling process can be executed in a lab environment without humidity control and there is no further requirement for parameter optimisation other than sample concentration.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation from the sample preparation protocol.

claim: The time from filling to vitrification was approximately 10 s in the experiments.
source: In our experiments, the total time from filling to vitrification was approximately 10 s.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental protocol.

claim: The checkerboard pattern structures the nanochannel array into a regular grid of 30 observation squares.
source: The checkerboard pattern from the silicon oxide layers on the observation membrane structures the nanochannel array into a regular grid of 30 observation squares, each comprising a segment of an individual nanochannel and flanking areas of the SiNx membrane (Figure 3a and b).
evidence: This is a description of the device design shown in Figure 3a and b.

claim: Up to 540 images can be acquired per cryoChip using the automated acquisition strategy.
source: For each of the acquisition points, three images were acquired radially around the midpoint using beam-image shift, resulting in up to 540 images per cryoChip.
evidence: This is calculated from the acquisition scheme: 30 observation squares × 6 acquisition points × 3 images = 540 images.

claim: 86% of ApoFtn images were classified as containing vitreous ice.
source: This led to a fraction of 86% (815/945), 75% (91/121), and 52% (43/82) of images that we classified as containing vitreous ice for ApoFtn, T20S and TMV respectively (Figure 4e, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct result from manual classification of images, shown in Figure 4e.

claim: 75% of T20S images were classified as containing vitreous ice.
source: This led to a fraction of 86% (815/945), 75% (91/121), and 52% (43/82) of images that we classified as containing vitreous ice for ApoFtn, T20S and TMV respectively (Figure 4e, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct result from manual classification of images, shown in Figure 4e.

claim: 52% of TMV images were classified as containing vitreous ice.
source: This led to a fraction of 86% (815/945), 75% (91/121), and 52% (43/82) of images that we classified as containing vitreous ice for ApoFtn, T20S and TMV respectively (Figure 4e, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct result from manual classification of images, shown in Figure 4e.

claim: Cooling below the glass-transition temperature occurs at timescales (< 10–5 seconds) compatible with vitrification according to convective heat-transfer simulations.
source: This is consistent with convective heat-transfer simulations of a simplified cryoChip model, suggesting that cooling below the glass-transition temperature occurs at timescales (< 10–5 seconds) compatible with vitrification (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a result from computational simulations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Evidence for hexagonal ice was found in non-vitreous images, indicating incomplete vitrification.
source: From a maximum intensity projection of all power spectra of all images, we find evidence for hexagonal ice indicating incomplete vitrification (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an analysis result from power spectra shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The ApoFtn dataset yielded a reconstruction at an overall resolution of 3.0 Å.
source: We used 2D and 3D classification to select a final set of 21,238 particles (O symmetry) from 815 micrographs and after 3D refinement obtained a reconstruction at an overall resolution of 3.0 Å displaying visible side chain densities (Figure 4c/d).
evidence: This is a direct result from single-particle analysis, shown in Figure 4c/d and Figure 4f.

claim: The TMV dataset yielded a 3D reconstruction at 3.7 Å resolution.
source: These datasets were collected on a JEOL JEM3200-FSC with a K2 detector and yielded 3D reconstructions with overall resolutions of 3.7 Å and 5.4 Å obtained from 14,238 segments (20 asu/segment) and 5750 particles (D7), respectively (Figure 4f, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a direct result from single-particle analysis, shown in Figure 4f.

claim: The T20S dataset yielded a 3D reconstruction at 5.4 Å resolution.
source: These datasets were collected on a JEOL JEM3200-FSC with a K2 detector and yielded 3D reconstructions with overall resolutions of 3.7 Å and 5.4 Å obtained from 14,238 segments (20 asu/segment) and 5750 particles (D7), respectively (Figure 4f, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a direct result from single-particle analysis, shown in Figure 4f.

claim: The quality of data collected from cryoChips is sufficient to allow initial model generation using the stochastic gradient descent method.
source: The reference model for 3D alignment was generated from the data itself using the stochastic gradient descent method (Figure 4—figure supplement 4), suggesting that the quality of data collected from cryoChips is sufficient to allow initial model generation even for samples considered difficult for reference model generation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by successful ab initio model generation from the cryoChip data.

claim: The B-factor for ApoFtn from cryoChips is 217 Å2.
source: This leads to B-factors of 217 Å2 vs. 178 Å2 for ApoFtn and 490 Å2 vs. 328 Å2 for T20S determined for cryoChip and holey carbon datasets, respectively.
evidence: This is calculated from ResLog analysis of the reconstruction data.

claim: The B-factor for T20S from cryoChips is 490 Å2.
source: This leads to B-factors of 217 Å2 vs. 178 Å2 for ApoFtn and 490 Å2 vs. 328 Å2 for T20S determined for cryoChip and holey carbon datasets, respectively.
evidence: This is calculated from ResLog analysis of the reconstruction data.

claim: Movement in cryoChips is largely unidirectional but clusters into several distinct directions of motion.
source: The calculated traces show that movement is largely unidirectional, but clusters into several distinct directions of motion.
evidence: This is observed from analysis of beam-induced motion trajectories shown in Figure 5.

claim: Three clusters of directional motion are observed for each chip, each associated with one of the three shot positions.
source: For each of the chips analysed, we observe three clusters of directional motion, each associated with one of the three shot positions.
evidence: This is observed from analysis of motion trajectories separated by chip and shot position, shown in Figure 5b and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The accumulated movement over 0–40 e-/Å2 ranges from 3.8 to 5.1 Å RMSD across different datasets.
source: The datasets show small differences in accumulated movement over the whole exposure, ranging from 3.8 (QF-R2/2) to 5.1 Å (cryoChip) RMSD over 0–40 e-/Å2.
evidence: This is calculated from RMSD analysis of motion trajectories shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Initial specimen movement of 1.8 Å is not limiting for achieving resolution beyond 2.0 Å.
source: EMPIAR-10389 led to a 2.0 Å reconstruction of Y. enterocolitica urease, indicating that initial specimen movement of that order is not limiting for achieving resolution beyond 2.0 Å.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with a reference dataset that achieved high resolution despite similar initial movement.

claim: The majority of particles are found close to or associated with the SiNx membrane in tomographic reconstructions.
source: In all cases, we find the majority of particles close to or associated with the SiNx membrane (Figure 6c, Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Figure 6—video 1).
evidence: This is observed from tomographic reconstructions shown in Figure 6c and supplementary figures.

claim: Increased abundance of views along the fourfold rotation axis was observed for ApoFtn, indicating preferential alignment with the SiNx membrane.
source: Analysis of the orientation distribution showed increased abundance of views along the fourfold rotation axis for ApoFtn, indicating preferential alignment of particles with the SiNx membrane (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is determined from Euler angle distribution analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: The particle concentration in the nanochannels is 262 µM or 126 mg/mL for ApoFtn.
source: We find 1483 ApoFtn particles within a 9.4 × 106 nm3 volume, equivalent to a concentration of 262 µM or 126 mg/mL assuming 480 kDa molecular mass.
evidence: This is calculated from particle counting and volume measurement in tomograms.

claim: The concentration in nanochannels represents a 37-fold increase compared to the initial sample concentration of 3.4 mg/mL.
source: This is a 37-fold increase in concentration compared to the initial sample concentration of 3.4 mg/mL.
evidence: This is calculated by comparing the measured concentration in nanochannels to the initial sample concentration.

claim: Interaction with the solid-liquid interface at the SiNx channel walls strongly affects the effective sample concentration in the nanochannels.
source: Interaction with the solid-liquid interface at the SiNx channel walls thus strongly affects the effective sample concentration in the nanochannels.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed concentration increase and particle distribution near the membrane.

claim: The SiNx membrane leads to additional background noise from an increase in the fraction of electrons that are scattered inelastically.
source: The SiNx membrane forming the walls of the nanochannels leads to additional background noise from an increase in the fraction of electrons that are scattered inelastically.
evidence: This is a known consequence of imaging through additional material, discussed in the context of image quality.

claim: The minimal scattering mass of particles that can be successfully detected and aligned under cryoChip conditions is estimated to be ~200 kDa.
source: By quantifying the additional scattering from the nanochannel membranes as an effective increase in ice thickness, we estimate the minimal scattering mass of particles that can still be successfully detected and aligned under these conditions to ~200 kDa (Henderson, 1995; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is estimated based on calculations of additional scattering and cited theoretical considerations.

claim: The cryoChip is fabricated using a sacrificial polysilicon process.
source: We used a sacrificial polysilicon process for fabrication of a device featuring nanofluidic channels for controlled cryo-EM sample preparation and imaging (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a description of the fabrication method, detailed in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The nanochannels are enclosed by ultrathin membranes made from silicon-rich nitride (SiNx).
source: The nanochannels are enclosed by ultrathin membranes made from silicon-rich nitride (SiNx) that allow for transmission of the electron beam when a thin film containing the sample is encapsulated in the space between them.
evidence: This is a description of the device materials and design.

claim: An aperture in the center of the silicon base exposes a 50 × 50 µm free-standing SiNx membrane.
source: An aperture in the center of the silicon base exposes a 50 × 50 µm free-standing SiNx membrane containing parallel rows of nanochannels that are connected to the central supply and exit channels via multifurcations.
evidence: This is a specification of the device design.

claim: The nanochannels are approximately 700 nm wide and 100 nm high.
source: A multifurcation connects the microchannels (blue) to an array of five parallel nanochannels (yellow) of approximately 700 nm width and 100 nm height (rightmost inset).
evidence: This is a specification of the nanochannel dimensions from the device design.

claim: The top membrane is smoothly sagging, while the bottom membrane is flat.
source: The top membrane is smoothly sagging, while the bottom membrane is flat.
evidence: This is a description of the membrane geometry observed in the fabricated devices.

claim: The mean free path for inelastic scattering at 300 keV in SiNx is 163 nm.
source: From the zero-loss log ratio of a SiNx area adjacent to the nanochannel (0.89) and the geometric film thickness determined by ellipsometry (19 nm, corresponding to the combined thickness of top and bottom membrane), we calculated the mean free path for inelastic scattering (IMFP) at 300 keV in SiNx as 163 nm, from which we estimate a combined water-equivalent thickness of 39 nm for the two SiNx membranes forming the nanochannel assuming an IMFP of 320 nm for vitreous ice (Yesibolati et al., 2020).
evidence: This is calculated from experimental measurements using zero-loss imaging.

claim: The precision of the sacrificial layer deposition permits tight control over the maximum channel height.
source: The precision of the sacrificial layer deposition in the fabrication process permits tight control over the maximum channel height.
evidence: This is inferred from the consistency of channel height measurements across chips.

claim: Manual handling of the syringe and the geometry of the nozzle currently limit the minimum droplet volume to about 10–40 nL.
source: Manual handling of the syringe and the geometry of the nozzle currently limit the minimum droplet volume to about 10–40 nL (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental setup and procedure.

claim: Residual sample of the filling droplet can be readily recovered.
source: Residual sample of the filling droplet can be readily recovered.
evidence: This is stated as a practical advantage of the filling method.

claim: High channel-to-channel reproducibility during fabrication is achieved.
source: We found similar behaviour across the chips that were analysed, suggesting that we can achieve high channel-to-channel reproducibility during fabrication (Figure 2d, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from consistent filling kinetics observed across multiple chips.

claim: There is no requirement for parameter optimisation other than sample concentration for cryoChip filling.
source: The entire filling process can be executed in a lab environment without humidity control and there is no further requirement for parameter optimisation other than sample concentration.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of the cryoChip method compared to conventional approaches.

claim: The cryoChip filling process could be readily accelerated by integrating the filling mechanism directly on a vitrification system.
source: This process could be readily accelerated by integrating the filling mechanism directly on a vitrification system.
evidence: This is a speculation about future improvements to the method.

claim: Most observation squares were suitable for data collection.
source: The low magnification maps revealed that most observation squares were suitable for data collection.
evidence: This is an observation from the data collection experiments.

claim: Partially broken or cracked membranes were occasionally observed.
source: We occasionally observed partially broken or cracked membranes. Observation squares in such areas were omitted for data collection.
evidence: This is an observation from the data collection experiments.

claim: Micrographs for all three specimens showed good image contrast.
source: Micrographs for all three specimens showed good image contrast (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is an observation from the acquired micrographs shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The fraction of vitreous images may be underestimated since discrimination between ice features from surface contamination and crystalline ice in nanochannels was not performed.
source: It is possible that the fraction of vitreous images is underestimated since we did not discriminate between ice features originating from surface contamination and those originating from crystalline ice in the nanochannels.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential sources of error in the vitrification efficiency analysis.

claim: No correlation was observed between the probability for forming crystalline ice and the location on the observation membrane.
source: We did not observe evidence for a correlation of the probability for forming crystalline ice and the location on the observation membrane.
evidence: This is an observation from analysis of the spatial distribution of icy images.

claim: High-contrast 2D class averages with visible features indicative of secondary structure were observed for all three specimens.
source: For all three specimens, we observe high-contrast 2D class averages with visible features indicative of secondary structure (Figure 4b, Figure 4—figure supplement 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 5, Figure 4—figure supplement 6), suggesting that images contain sufficient contrast for high-resolution structure determination.
evidence: This is observed from 2D classification results shown in Figure 4b and supplementary figures.

claim: The ApoFtn reconstruction displays visible side chain densities.
source: We used 2D and 3D classification to select a final set of 21,238 particles (O symmetry) from 815 micrographs and after 3D refinement obtained a reconstruction at an overall resolution of 3.0 Å displaying visible side chain densities (Figure 4c/d).
evidence: This is observed in the 3D reconstruction shown in Figure 4c/d.

claim: There is a consistent upward shift of the offset for holey carbon B-factor plots compared to those from cryoChips.
source: We also note a consistent upward shift of the offset for holey carbon B-factor plots compared to those from cryoChips, consistent with the differences in overall signal-to-noise ratio caused by additional scattering from the SiNx membrane.
evidence: This is observed from comparison of B-factor plots shown in Figure 4g and Figure 4—figure supplement 7.

claim: The highest rate of change in particle position is typically largest at cumulative exposures below ~4e-/Å2.
source: The highest rate of change in particle position is typically largest at cumulative exposures below ~4e-/Å2 (Vinothkumar and Henderson, 2016), coinciding with the frames where the sample is yet least affected by radiation damage and high-resolution signal is best preserved.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field, supported by citation.

claim: Movement in cryoChips is largely unidirectional but clusters into several distinct directions of motion associated with beam-image shift positions.
source: The calculated traces show that movement is largely unidirectional, but clusters into several distinct directions of motion. To further investigate the trajectories, we separated them either by chip or by the beam-image shift condition corresponding to the shot position in the multishot acquisition scheme for each acquisition point (Figure 5b, Figure 5—figure supplement 1). For each of the chips analysed, we observe three clusters of directional motion, each associated with one of the three shot positions.
evidence: This is observed from analysis of motion trajectories shown in Figure 5b and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Different thickness and geometry of the confined ice layer in subregions may lead to preferential directionality of specimen movement.
source: While the precise origin for this clustering needs further investigation, we suggest that different thickness and geometry of the confined ice layer in the subregions for each of the multishot positions may lead to preferential directionality of specimen movement, possibly combined with microlensing effects resulting from adjacent exposures that induce the build-up of semi-static charge on the non-conductive SiNx membrane.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism underlying the observed directional clustering of motion.

claim: Overall specimen movement ranges from 3.8 to 5.1 Å RMSD over 0–40 e-/Å2 for different datasets.
source: The datasets show small differences in accumulated movement over the whole exposure, ranging from 3.8 (QF-R2/2) to 5.1 Å (cryoChip) RMSD over 0–40 e-/Å2.
evidence: This is calculated from RMSD analysis of motion trajectories shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Overall motions represent a combination of mechanical (stage) drift and beam-induced motion.
source: These overall motions represent a combination of mechanical (stage) drift and beam-induced motion.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the observed specimen movement.

claim: Initial specimen movement of 1.8 Å was observed for both the cryoChip dataset and EMPIAR-10389.
source: EMPIAR-10306 has a remarkably low initial movement of 0.7 Å, while both our dataset and EMPIAR-10389 display a accumulated motion of 1.8 Å.
evidence: This is measured from motion trajectory analysis shown in Figure 5d.

claim: The closed sample environment of the cryoChip avoids the problems of an air-water interface.
source: The closed sample environment of the cryoChip avoids the problems of an air-water interface, but the large surface-to-volume ratio of the nanochannels forms an extensive solid-liquid interface between the SiNx surface and the particle solution.
evidence: This is a description of the design feature and its consequence.

claim: The large surface-to-volume ratio of the nanochannels forms an extensive solid-liquid interface between the SiNx surface and the particle solution.
source: The closed sample environment of the cryoChip avoids the problems of an air-water interface, but the large surface-to-volume ratio of the nanochannels forms an extensive solid-liquid interface between the SiNx surface and the particle solution.
evidence: This is a geometric consequence of the nanochannel design.

claim: Tomographic reconstructions confirm the overall geometry of the channels with an estimated height ranging between 0 and 100 nm and a channel width of ~750 nm.
source: The tomographic reconstructions confirm the overall geometry of the channels with an estimated height in cross-section ranging between 0 and 100 nm and a channel width of ~750 nm (Figure 6a/b).
evidence: This is measured from tomographic reconstructions shown in Figure 6a/b.

claim: Preferential abundance of side views was found for T20S particles.
source: Similarly, we find preferential abundance of side views for T20S particles (Figure 4—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is observed from Euler angle distribution analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 6.

claim: No convincing correlation of preferred orientations with the molecular electrostatic potential was observed.
source: We did not observe convincing correlation of preferred orientations with the molecular electrostatic potential (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated as a result from analysis comparing orientation distributions with electrostatic potential maps.

claim: Particle densities in micrographs exceed those expected from conventional cryo-EM grids prepared with the same specimens and sample concentrations.
source: Micrographs from datasets of all three specimen display particle densities exceeding those expected from conventional cryo-EM grids prepared with the same specimens and sample concentrations.
evidence: This is an observation from visual inspection of micrographs and quantitative analysis.

claim: Interaction with the solid-liquid interface at the SiNx channel walls strongly affects the effective sample concentration in the nanochannels.
source: Interaction with the solid-liquid interface at the SiNx channel walls thus strongly affects the effective sample concentration in the nanochannels.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed 37-fold concentration increase.

claim: Similar concentration effects have been reported for traditional sample preparation methods such as repeated sample application.
source: Similar concentration effects have also been reported for traditional sample preparation methods, such as repeated sample application (Snijder et al., 2017) and in the presence of very thin ice for which densely packed protein monolayers have been observed (Yip et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature reporting similar phenomena.

claim: Sample preparation is widely perceived as a major bottleneck for realising the full potential of cryo-EM.
source: The process of sample preparation is widely perceived as a major bottleneck for realising the full potential of cryo-EM.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: All existing approaches to cryo-EM sample preparation rely on the ill-controlled formation of thin ice layers across fenestrated support films.
source: All existing approaches to cryo-EM sample preparation rely on the ill-controlled formation of thin ice layers across fenestrated support films, which results in poor reproducibility and may detrimentally affect particle distribution, orientation and integrity (D'Imprima et al., 2019; Noble et al., 2018; Glaeser and Han, 2017; Glaeser, 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a characterization of current methods, supported by citations.

claim: MEMS-based nanofluidic chips provide a viable alternative for cryo-EM sample preparation that mitigates some prevalent issues observed for grid-based sample supports.
source: Here, we have shown that MEMS-based nanofluidic chips in which the sample is enclosed and protected from the air-water interface within electron-transparent nanochannels provide a viable alternative for cryo-EM sample preparation that mitigates some of the prevalent issues observed for grid-based sample supports.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the experimental results presented.

claim: Biological specimens in cryoChips can be successfully vitrified.
source: We demonstrated that biological specimens in cryoChips can be successfully vitrified and that the thickness uniformity of the ice layer can be reproducibly controlled by channel geometry.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the successful structure determination from vitrified samples.

claim: The thickness uniformity of the ice layer can be reproducibly controlled by channel geometry.
source: We demonstrated that biological specimens in cryoChips can be successfully vitrified and that the thickness uniformity of the ice layer can be reproducibly controlled by channel geometry.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the ice thickness measurements showing consistent profiles across chips.

claim: The width and height of the nanochannels are highly consistent across individual cryoChips.
source: We found the width and height of the nanochannels to be highly consistent across individual cryoChips, providing uniform imaging conditions for all parts of a chip.
evidence: This is demonstrated by measurements shown in Figure 1f.

claim: The most widely applied methods for cryo-EM sample preparation currently require ~3 µL of sample volume per grid.
source: The most widely applied methods for cryo-EM sample preparation currently require ~3 µL of sample volume per grid.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about conventional methods.

claim: The required sample volume for imaging is only 1.5–7.0 fL for conventional methods, which is nine orders of magnitude less than the initial sample volume.
source: Assuming a final liquid film of 20–100 nm thickness spanning a 3.05 mm EM support grid, the required sample volume for imaging is only 1.5–7.0 fL, which is nine orders of magnitude less than the initial sample volume.
evidence: This is calculated from the geometry of conventional sample supports.

claim: The cryoChip reduces the required sample volume by 1000-fold compared to recent developments to only a few picoliters.
source: The cryoChip presented here further reduces the required sample volume by 1000-fold to only a few picoliters, approaching the practical minimum for liquid handling in cryo-EM structure determination.
evidence: This is calculated from the estimated filling volume of ~4 pL compared to nanoliter volumes of other methods.

claim: The cantilever-based sample application efficiently drives chip filling via capillary action, allowing essentially loss-less cryo-EM sample preparation.
source: The cantilever-based sample application efficiently drives chip filling via capillary action, thus allowing essentially loss-less cryo-EM sample preparation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the filling experiments and the ability to recover residual sample.

claim: Sample preparation using cryoChips does not require humidity control.
source: Notably, sample preparation using cryoChips does not require humidity control and is compatible with any standard plunger available in cryo-EM laboratories.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of the method based on experimental observations.

claim: Ab initio structure determination was demonstrated for three different test specimens resolved at resolutions suitable for mechanistic interpretation.
source: Using cryoChip supports, we demonstrated ab initio structure determination for three different test specimen resolved at resolutions suitable for mechanistic interpretation even from datasets with a comparatively small set of particles.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the successful structure determination results presented.

claim: Between 10% and 40% of images contain non-vitreous ice despite predictions from heat transfer simulations.
source: Despite our predictions from heat transfer simulations, we observed that between 10% and 40% of images contain non-vitreous ice.
evidence: This is calculated from the vitrification efficiency analysis showing 52-86% vitreous images.

claim: Cryogen may be displaced by the chip base upon entering the cryogen, preventing complete wetting of the chip.
source: Firstly, it is possible that cryogen is displaced by the chip base upon entering the cryogen, preventing complete wetting of the chip; or that air is trapped in the depression on the chip base below the free-standing observation membrane, preventing contact with the coolant and impeding heat transfer from the nanochannels.
evidence: This is speculation about possible causes for incomplete vitrification.

claim: The observation membrane is located at the chip center which could affect probability of vitrification.
source: Secondly, the observation membrane is located at the chip center which could affect probability of vitrification, consistent with the spatial distribution of isotherms reported for standard holey film grids during immersion cooling (Kasas et al., 2003).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation to literature on cooling dynamics.

claim: Different plunging speed or depth, or jet-based cooling, may be more appropriate for cryoChips.
source: Parameters for existing plunging instruments have been optimised to maximise vitrification efficiency for holey film supports and it is conceivable that different plunging speed or depth, or jet-based cooling, may be more appropriate for cryoChips.
evidence: This is speculation about potential improvements to the vitrification process.

claim: The concave cross-sectional shape of the nanochannel produces a defined thickness gradient within which particles naturally partition into monolayers.
source: In cryoChips, the concave cross-sectional shape of the nanochannel produces a defined thickness gradient within which particles naturally partition into monolayers according to their molecular dimensions in the thinner parts of the channel, thus minimising background scattering from surrounding ice.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed ice thickness gradient and particle distribution in tomograms.

claim: The sample confinement in cryoChip nanochannels comes with the penalty of additional incoherent scattering from the enclosing SiNx membranes.
source: The sample confinement in cryoChip nanochannels, however, comes with the penalty of additional incoherent scattering from the enclosing SiNx membranes, which results in reduced image contrast compared to ideal samples.
evidence: This is a known consequence of imaging through additional material, discussed in the context of image quality.

claim: CryoChips should be suitable for imaging a wide range of relevant protein targets for cryo-EM structure determination with molecular mass ~200 kDa and above.
source: By quantifying the additional scattering from the nanochannel membranes as an effective increase in ice thickness, we estimate the minimal scattering mass of particles that can still be successfully detected and aligned under these conditions to ~200 kDa (Henderson, 1995; Zhang et al., 2020). This should render cryoChips suitable for imaging a wide range of relevant protein targets for cryo-EM structure determination.
evidence: This is inferred from calculations of additional scattering and cited theoretical considerations.

claim: Spectral properties of structural noise contributed by the SiNx membranes are different from those of vitreous ice.
source: Apart from incoherent scattering contributions by the SiNx membrane, several other factors may currently limit resolution: Firstly, spectral properties of structural noise contributed by the SiNx membranes are different from those of vitreous ice, and secondly, there may be interference of signal from SiNx membranes and particles located at different focal heights within the nanochannel that may affect accuracy of CTF estimation (Tichelaar et al., 2020, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is discussed as a potential limitation, supported by citation and analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: There may be interference of signal from SiNx membranes and particles located at different focal heights within the nanochannel that may affect accuracy of CTF estimation.
source: Apart from incoherent scattering contributions by the SiNx membrane, several other factors may currently limit resolution: Firstly, spectral properties of structural noise contributed by the SiNx membranes are different from those of vitreous ice, and secondly, there may be interference of signal from SiNx membranes and particles located at different focal heights within the nanochannel that may affect accuracy of CTF estimation (Tichelaar et al., 2020, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is discussed as a potential limitation, supported by citation and analysis.

claim: Assumptions on image statistics in current 3D reconstruction algorithms may be sub-optimal for particles from cryoChips.
source: It is possible that assumptions on image statistics in current 3D reconstruction algorithms are sub-optimal for particles from cryoChips and improvements could be gained with modified software.
evidence: This is speculation about potential software improvements.

claim: Nanochannels are closed volumes implying that molecular hydrogen formed as a product of electron-beam induced radiolysis cannot escape.
source: First, nanochannels are closed volumes implying that molecular hydrogen formed as a product of electron-beam induced radiolysis (Aronova et al., 2011) cannot escape.
evidence: This is inferred from the closed architecture of the nanochannels and cited knowledge about radiolysis.

claim: Trapped gas may lead to pressure build-up inside the nanochannel and ultimately specimen movement.
source: Trapped gas may lead to pressure build-up inside the nanochannel and ultimately specimen movement.
evidence: This is speculation about a potential mechanism for beam-induced motion.

claim: Overall specimen movement in cryoChips is higher than for modified support films.
source: While we found overall specimen movement in cryoChips to be higher than for modified support films, the residual particle displacement is not limiting for ~2 Å reconstructions and hence in a range suitable for high-resolution map interpretation.
evidence: This is observed from comparison of motion trajectories with reference datasets.

claim: The residual particle displacement in cryoChips is not limiting for ~2 Å reconstructions.
source: While we found overall specimen movement in cryoChips to be higher than for modified support films, the residual particle displacement is not limiting for ~2 Å reconstructions and hence in a range suitable for high-resolution map interpretation.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with reference datasets that achieved high resolution with similar motion.

claim: The air-water interface is hydrophobic and adsorption of proteins to the interface can drive partial or complete unfolding.
source: The air-water interface is hydrophobic and adsorption of proteins to the interface can drive partial or complete unfolding to minimise the free energy of interaction (Glaeser, 2018; D'Imprima et al., 2019; Noble et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: The polar SiNx surface is hydrophilic and adsorption of proteins is primarily mediated by the zeta potential of the interfacial electrical double layer.
source: In contrast, similar to oxidised graphene, the polar SiNx surface is hydrophilic and adsorption of proteins is primarily mediated by the zeta potential of the interfacial electrical double layer (Norde, 1986).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about protein-surface interactions, supported by citation.

claim: For the three cases investigated, the interaction with SiNx does not promote denaturation or aberrant structural changes.
source: Consistently, for the three cases we investigated we do not observe that this interaction promotes denaturation or aberrant structural changes.
evidence: This is inferred from the successful high-resolution structure determination without evidence of denaturation.

claim: The charge distribution between the molecular electrostatic potential and at the solid-liquid interface could promote preferential alignment.
source: It is entirely possible that the charge distribution between the molecular electrostatic potential and at the solid-liquid interface could promote preferential alignment and hence carry the risk of systematic bias in particle orientation.
evidence: This is speculation about a potential mechanism for preferred orientation.

claim: No pronounced preferred orientation was found for the cases studied.
source: For the cases studied we did not find evidence for pronounced preferred orientation and could not identify strong correlation of enriched views with the molecular electrostatic potential.
evidence: This is stated as a result from orientation distribution analysis.

claim: The current analysis is limited to particles with internal symmetry for which preferred orientations are less problematic.
source: We note that the current analysis is limited to particles with internal symmetry for which preferred orientations are less problematic.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the current study.

claim: Further investigation will be required to conclude whether systematic effects for preferred protein adsorption to the solid-liquid interface exist.
source: Further investigation will be required to conclude whether systematic effects for preferred protein adsorption to the solid-liquid interface exist and need to be addressed.
evidence: This is stated as a need for future research.

claim: The strong interaction at the solid-liquid interface is principally beneficial for concentrating dilute protein solutions to particle densities suitable for imaging.
source: While this is principally beneficial for concentrating dilute protein solutions to particle densities suitable for imaging, it also affects design considerations for the filling channels.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed concentration effect.

claim: Early design iterations featured narrow filling and exit channels and showed apparent depletion of the protein sample before it reached the observation nanochannels.
source: In early design iterations of the cryoChips that featured narrow filling and exit channels, we observed apparent depletion of the protein sample before it reached the observation nanochannels.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from earlier experiments.

claim: The very large surface-to-volume ratio of nanochannels may deplete solute proteins through interactions with the SiN walls in the filling channel.
source: We attribute this to the very large surface-to-volume ratio of nanochannels, which we suspect may bear the risk to deplete solute proteins through interactions with the SiN walls in the filling channel, thus gradually reducing the free protein concentration in solution as they travel towards the observation membrane.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism for protein depletion in narrow channels.

claim: The increased diameter of the filling channel in the current cryoChip design substantially improved the efficacy for reaching suitable particle concentrations in the nanochannels.
source: The increased diameter of the filling channel in the current cryoChip design substantially improved the efficacy for reaching suitable particle concentrations in the nanochannels of the observation membrane.
evidence: This is stated as a design improvement based on observations.

claim: Further studies are needed to reveal the detailed dynamics and underlying mechanisms of particle adsorption to solid-liquid interfaces.
source: With solid-liquid interfaces gaining importance also for existing cryo-EM supports (D'Imprima et al., 2019; Naydenova et al., 2019; Naydenova et al., 2020), further studies are needed to reveal the detailed dynamics and underlying mechanisms of particle adsorption to such interfaces, and to systematically investigate their effects on particle integrity and orientation.
evidence: This is stated as a need for future research.

claim: Continuous developments have pushed the limit of achievable contrast and residual specimen movement for holey support films.
source: Just as continuous developments have pushed the limit of achievable contrast and residual specimen movement for holey support films (Naydenova et al., 2020), we expect that similar progress can be attained for nanofluidic supports by further improvements in electron transparency, as well as electrical and thermal conductance of the enclosing materials.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by citation.

claim: Similar progress can be attained for nanofluidic supports by further improvements in electron transparency, as well as electrical and thermal conductance of the enclosing materials.
source: Just as continuous developments have pushed the limit of achievable contrast and residual specimen movement for holey support films (Naydenova et al., 2020), we expect that similar progress can be attained for nanofluidic supports by further improvements in electron transparency, as well as electrical and thermal conductance of the enclosing materials.
evidence: This is speculation about future improvements.

claim: Ongoing developments will eventually allow approaching resolutions and conditions realised for ideal samples.
source: We anticipate that ongoing developments will eventually allow approaching resolutions and conditions realised for ideal samples (Zivanov et al., 2018).
evidence: This is speculation about future improvements, supported by citation to ideal sample results.

claim: The cryoChip is only the beginning of a range of future cryo-EM supports building on MEMS technology.
source: We predict that the cryoChip is only the beginning of a range of future cryo-EM supports building on MEMS technology.
evidence: This is speculation about future developments.

claim: The observation membrane currently represents less than 0.1% of the entire chip area.
source: Currently the observation membrane is 50 µm x 50 µm, representing less than 0.1% of the entire chip area.
evidence: This is calculated from the chip dimensions (2 mm × 2 mm = 4 mm² vs. 50 µm × 50 µm = 0.0025 mm²).

claim: The imaging area can be readily extended by additional observation membranes.
source: The imaging area can be readily extended by additional observation membranes, thus allowing fully automated collection of thousands of images with uniform ice thickness from a single chip.
evidence: This is speculation about future design improvements.

claim: Parallel arrangements of observation membranes with separate filling channels will allow screening different samples on the same chip.
source: Parallel arrangements of observation membranes with separate filling channels will allow screening different samples on the same chip.
evidence: This is speculation about future design possibilities.

claim: The versatility of nanofabrication technology opens up possibilities to facilitate a range of new cryo-EM applications.
source: Beyond this, the versatility of nanofabrication technology opens up possibilities to facilitate a range of new cryo-EM applications by bridging lab-on-a-chip approaches with structural biology. These include possibilities for on-chip mixing, parallelised high-throughput screening for structure-based drug discovery, time-resolved experiments, on-chip purification of complex protein mixtures and the combination of structure determination with biophysical measurements.
evidence: This is speculation about future applications enabled by the technology.
